the more I love him.

PREFACE.

The 1855 edition of the Dhammapada being exhausted, I have considered it advisable to publish the book again, but in an abridged form intended particularly for young students who wish to take up the study of Pāli.

For I am convinced that you can scarcely find a book better suited for introducing beginners to the Pāli language and Buddhist Pāli literature than this one, its style being accessible and its sayings striking, and furthermore it containing some of the core tenets of the Buddhist religion.

I have retained the literal Latin translation, improving it slightly here and there. I consider a literal translation an essential aid to understanding the text, especially for beginners, and it may sometimes also be useful for more advanced readers who wish to penetrate into the true meaning of a disputed verse.

But I have left out nearly all the linguistic explanations found in the 1855 edition, referring to it only occasionally, since those explanations have been incorporated into later European Pāli grammars.

As to the editing of the Text, I have departed from my old method of giving the traditional

VI

text. I have followed a new principle, namely, to let not only analogy and parallelism but especially the Metre guide me in restoring the verses to their original form, a principle which in due time will also be applied to the text of the Vedas.

For it is clear that, if we find, for example, verses in all the manuscripts traditionally written as follows:
Upeto damasaccena sa ve kāsāvam arahati, see verses 9, 10, 230; compare 98, 30.
sādhu dassanam ariyānam, v. 206.
Yathāpi rahado gambhīro vippasanno anāvilo, v. 82.
Evam bho purisa jānāhi v. 248.
Na câhu na ca bhavissati, v. 228.
Na tena bhikkhu hoti yāvatā bhikkhate pare, v. 266, etc. etc. see Appendix to the Edition of the Dhammapada of 1855,
then these verses must have been corrupted by the transcribers who carelessly substituted one form of a word for another, generally a later form, but sometimes also an older one.

This can be proved partly by the metre being incorrect, as in the verses cited above, and partly by the correct forms having been preserved in other verses, for example:
Pariyodapeyya attānam cittaklesehi paṇḍito (later kilesehi), v. 88.
Ārāmarukkhacetyāni (later cetyāni), v. 188.
Pathavyā ekarajjena (later paṭhaviyā), v. 178.
I think therefore we may feel justified in correcting the text by re-adopting old forms, for example vajra

VII

v. 161, bhavati v. 260, thaviro v. 261, khatyo v. 387, poso v. 228. 248, or by sometimes choosing a later form, for instance pibenti v. 181, hessati v. 228*, in order to make the metre correct. And this is what I have done in constituting the text.

Also the rules of Sandhi (vowel and consonant combination) are in the manuscripts sometimes kept and sometimes neglected. Here again the metre must decide what we are to read, for instance:

In v. 89 the manuscripts and the Singhalese Edition rightly read sambodhiañgesu, but the Burmese Edition prints sambodhiyañgesu; in later Pāli it would be sambojjhañgesu. In v. 175 we must of course read haṁsādiccapathe and not haṁsā ādicca-; in v. 318 câvajja- and not ca avajja-, etc. In v. 125 I have corrected pacceti** to paṭieti, but I am not quite sure of being right in this case, as it seems that the metrical pattern — — — may be allowed in this pada instead of ‒ ⌣ ‒ ‒; but if I am right we must also read sāmaṇiyassa in v. 19, pajināvudhena in v. 40, tasiṇā in v. 349, cf. v. 342; and in the Suttanipāta v. 83 dhammasuāmi, v. 89 katuāna. In v. 137 we must read dasann' against both the manuscripts and the Editions, in v. 210 piyān', in v. 333 pāpān', like mal' itthiyā v. 242, and so on.

IX

EDITIONS OF THE TEXT.

Since the publication of the
1. Dhammapadam. Edited from three Copenhagen manuscripts in Pali, translated into Latin, and illustrated with excerpts from the Pali commentary and notes by V. Fausbøll. Copenhagen, 1855.
there have appeared the following editions:
2. The Dhammapada or Principles of Morality. With a Singhalese Translation. Revised by the Reverend H. Devamittâ. Colombo, 1879. (In Singhalese characters).
3. Dhammapada Pālito. Rangoon. Burmese Era 1242. (In Burmese characters).
4. The Text of the Dhammapada is also to be found in the 25th volume of the King of Siam's Edition of the Tipitaka*, containing the Khuddakapāṭha, the Dhammapada, the Udāna, the Itivuttaka and the Suttanipāta.

* It is strange to see Pāli books printed in modern Siamese type, with which Pāli manuscripts were never written, and which is also very hard on the eyes on account of the thinness of the letters. If the edition had been printed in Roman characters it would certainly have advanced scholarship; now I am afraid it will be rather a hindrance to it. There can be no doubt that the Roman (Latin) character will ultimately triumph over all others.
The most widely used scripts are:
the Roman, which is used by approximately 394 million people
the Chinese, approximately 391 million
the Indian, with its descendants, approximately 311 million.
And just as certainly as the Roman character will become universal, the English language will in time likewise become the universal language of the world — for it is a well known fact that in the beginning the Lord took all languages, boiled them in a pot, and forthwith extracted the English language as the essence of them all.

DHAMMAPADA.

1. The Pairs (Yamakavagga)

1. Mind is the forerunner of all actions, mind is their chief, they are mind-made. If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, suffering follows, as the wheel follows the hoof of an ox.

2. Mind is the forerunner of all actions, mind is their chief, they are mind-made. If one speaks or acts with a serene mind, happiness follows, like a shadow that never departs.

3. "He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me" — in those who harbor such thoughts, hatred will never cease.

4. "He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me" — in those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred will quickly cease.

5. Never in this world is hatred settled by hatred; it is only settled by non-hatred. This is an eternal law.

6. Others do not understand that in this quarrel we are all heading toward death; those who do understand it — their quarrels cease at once.

7. One who dwells contemplating what is pleasant, unrestrained in the senses, immoderate in eating, lazy and lacking in energy — Mara will surely overpower him, as the wind bends a weak tree.

2. The Chapter on Heedfulness.

21. Heedfulness is the path to the deathless; heedlessness is the path to death. Those who are heedful do not die; those who are heedless are as if already dead.

22. Having clearly understood this distinction, the wise delight in heedfulness, rejoicing in the domain of the noble ones.

23. Those meditators who are steadfast and persistent, the resolute and wise, touch Nibbana — the supreme freedom from bondage.

24. For one who is energetic, mindful, pure in action, and acting with deliberation —

[Footnotes: Variant readings from manuscript traditions B, C, and S for verses 18–20, with cross-references to the Suttanipata and Samyutta Nikaya.]

He who has done good rejoices in both worlds; "good has been done by me," thinking thus he rejoices, and rejoices even more upon entering heaven. Yet if a lazy man speaks many fine words but does not act on them, like a cowherd who merely counts other people's cattle, he does not become a member of the community of Samanas. But if someone speaks few fine words yet lives according to the law, and abandoning desire, hatred, and mental disturbance, truly wise, endowed with a well-liberated mind, desiring nothing here or there — he does become a member of the community of Samanas.

Chapter 2.

Diligence is the path to immortality; negligence is the path to death. The diligent do not die; those who are negligent are as if already dead. Those who clearly understand this, being wise in diligence, rejoice in diligence, delighting in the lot of the noble. These, being meditative and persevering, always endowed with strong effort, the wise attain Nibbana, the highest happiness. For one who strives, who remembers, who works honestly, who acts with care, who gathers himself together —

Of one who is restrained and lives by the Dhamma,
the fame of the diligent one grows.

25. Through effort, diligence, discipline, and self-control,
let the wise one make an island that no flood can overwhelm.

26. Fools and people of poor understanding devote themselves to negligence,
but the wise one guards diligence as the greatest treasure.

27. Do not give yourself over to negligence, do not be intimate with sensual pleasure;
for the one who meditates diligently attains abundant happiness.

28. When the wise one dispels negligence through diligence,
having ascended the high tower of wisdom, free from sorrow, he looks upon the sorrowing crowd—
as one standing on a mountain looks down upon those standing on the ground, the wise one looks upon the fools.

29. Among the negligent, the diligent one; among the sleeping, the wide-awake one—
like a swift horse leaving a weak one behind, the person of good wisdom moves forward.

30. By diligence, Maghava attained the highest rank among the gods;
diligence is always praised, negligence is always blamed.

31. The monk who delights in diligence, who sees danger in negligence,
burns up every fetter, great and small, like a fire.

32. The monk who delights in diligence, who sees danger in negligence,
is incapable of falling away—he is in the very presence of Nibbana.

     do not swallow a ball of iron while heedless,
     do not cry out "this is suffering!" while burning.

372. There is no meditation for one without wisdom, and no wisdom for one who does not meditate;
     one in whom both meditation and wisdom are present is truly close to Nibbāna.
